title: Pack manifest
description: A pack's declaration of what it needs, what it provides and what it may do. 1.2.0 closed the behaviour clause to `name, trigger, condition, action, priority, services, slots` -- and every one of those names a *kind*, with no value anywhere: a behaviour could say `condition: state` and could not say *which* state, could say `action: service` and could not say which mode to enter, and a pack could declare what it does and not one number about how. 1.3.0 added the values and the one clause that makes a pack configurable. `match` is the value beside a state condition -- the readings the behaviour acts on; `mode` is the value beside a service action whose act is entering a house mode rather than writing an entity; `for` names a duration option and turns its `match` from 'is open' into 'has been open this long'; `slots` lets a pack declare a device the catalog does not name; and `options` is how a pack offers a person a number, a switch or a choice at all, each typed so the panel can draw the right control for it. All five are optional, so every 1.2.0 pack is a 1.3.0 pack; and none is an expression, so the declarative-only property 1.2.0 established is unchanged: a value is a literal the vocabulary can check, not a template the engine must evaluate. 1.4.0 adds `suppresses`, and it is the first clause that lets a pack reach *another* pack. A behaviour naming packs here holds them off for as long as it is on -- the module-level override a pack places over a pack, which the engine derives from which modules are currently on rather than writing down, so it is temporary by construction and undone the moment either switch moves. It names whole packs and nothing finer, because switching a module off is the one act that changes nothing about the target and so the one act installation can always reverse; a clause reaching deeper would be a pack editing another pack's configuration. A pack may not name itself: a pack that holds itself off can never run, and its own switch is what turns a pack off. The clause is optional, so every 1.3.0 pack is a 1.4.0 pack.

kind.description: The kind of pack this is. 1.1.0 carried this as a pattern and said why in its own words -- "A pattern and not an enum because no corpus of packs exists to derive a closed set of kinds from, and inventing one here would freeze..." -- and 1.2.0 ships that corpus, so the closure is this version's to make.

requires_slots.description: Slot names, resolved against slots.yaml. A pack that names a slot no slot file defines is a pack that cannot be installed anywhere. Required for the kinds that are plugged into a room and forbidden nowhere; the per-kind conditionals below say which kinds must carry it. The list may be empty, and an empty list is a statement rather than a hole: a pack that acts through a service and no placeholder -- a notification, an alarm panel, a siren -- is plugged into a room and needs nothing of it. The home's own state used to be the slot that made such packs non-empty, and it is the engine's variable rather than a device anybody binds, so a corpus row that required it now requires nothing and says so.

optional_slots.description: Slots the pack can use but does not require, so a house missing one still installs it. Separate from `requires_slots` rather than folded in, because the two say different things about the house the pack lands in and one list cannot carry both.

slots.description: The slots this pack brings with it. A pack may need a device no catalog slot names -- a fridge's door, a freezer's -- and the vocabulary is grown by the modules rather than by a publisher's release, so the pack that needs the reading declares it and fixes the domains a binding may use. A declared name says what the device is: two packs naming the same slot share the one device, so the name is the whole of the disambiguation -- there is no second sentence to fall back on, which is why a name that could mean two devices is the defect this clause exists to refuse.

provides.description: Every entry carries the artifact class it confers, because the class-pinning rule is what stops a pack smuggling an unpinnable artifact past the licence gate by calling it a helper.

behaviours.description: The behaviours the pack declares, each named by a trigger, a condition and an action drawn from `behavior-vocabulary`'s published axes. The terms are referenced, not restated, so the pack cannot use a behaviour term the vocabulary does not carry. Required for the kinds that do something in a room; a template declares what a room has rather than what it does, so the per-kind conditionals below forbid it there.

options.description: The settings this pack offers a person, each a small typed declaration and never a free-form schema. A module knows what it is *for* and what a person might reasonably want to change about it -- how long the fridge door may stand open, whether the fan runs at all after dark -- and until this clause existed there was nowhere to say so: a pack could declare what it does and not one number about how. The declaration is deliberately narrow rather than a nested JSON Schema, because the panel already renders a schema and the interesting question is not what *can* be expressed but what the *engine* will act on. Every option resolves under `module.<pack>.<key>` through the same layered resolver as every other tunable (`engine/config.py`), so a house and a room may each set one and the pack's `default` is the bottom of the stack. **An option is only worth declaring if something reads it**: `for` on a behaviour names a duration option and is how the declarative interpreter acts on one, and a boolean option's honest use is gated the same way. Declaring an option nothing reads is the defect this description exists to warn against, because the panel will render a control for it and the control will do nothing.

dependencies.description: Installed packs this pack needs, each an installed pack's name and a semver range its version must satisfy. Resolved against the house's installed set and never against the repository, because what a pack may rely on is what the house actually holds.

conflicts.description: Packs this pack must not share a house with, each a name and a range it must not satisfy. Checked in both directions -- from the arriving pack to the installed set and from each installed pack to the arriving one -- because a conflict one pack states and the other does not is still a conflict.

engine_api.description: The engine API range this pack is written for, as a semver range: comparators over dotted versions, joined by whitespace or `||`. It supersedes `min_engine_version`, which pinned a lower bound and could not express an upper one, so a pack broken by the next major version could not say so. Checked against the engine's own declared API version, which is published in an artifact of its own rather than read from `pyproject.toml` -- whose `version` is `0.0.0` and moves for packaging reasons, which would make every range a lie.

license.description: The pack's licence, as one of the codes `schemas/catalog/licenses.json` publishes -- the same codes `catalog/behaviors.yaml`'s rows already speak, so a manifest that said `MIT` would be a third spelling of one fact. Each code carries its SPDX identifier in that artifact rather than in a second list here.

i18n.description: A default string for every user-visible name the pack declares, with locale overrides resolved over it. Required rather than optional, because a name with no default is a name some locale cannot render.

derives_from.description: The corpus row ids this pack reproduces expression from, read against `catalog/behaviors.yaml`. Carried by a derived pack and forbidden on a hand-written one, because a file a person wrote reproduces no row's expression -- provenance that lives only in a report on the machine that ran the derivation stops travelling the moment the pack is copied, and an empty list is not a derivation.

then.description: A module is the kind that does something in a room: it is plugged into the room's placeholders and it carries the behaviours that act through them.

provides.description: A module provides automations, scripts and scenes; a mode is what a profile-set confers, so the class is refused here rather than left to a convention.

then.description: A behaviour pack is one behaviour offered on its own, so it carries exactly one and the slots it acts through.
A room template declares what a room has -- its slots and the room type it reproduces -- and not what it does, so it carries no behaviours of its own.

A house template declares the house a pack set lands in -- the slots the whole house offers, read from the room catalog's house entry -- and not what any room does, so it carries no behaviours of its own.

A profile-set confers a mode -- the state a behaviour is gated on, which is what `schemas/mode/1.0.0.json` fixes and what the engine already enforces exclusivity over. It must provide at least one, or it confers nothing.

path.description: Repo-relative path. A string fact, so its shape comes from `schemas/catalog/fact-shapes.yaml` shared by every filed fact. Resolved against the repository root and required to stay inside the pack's own directory -- resolving against the root is only sound if the answer is still inside the pack.

class.description: The artifact class this entry confers, drawn from the closed class set rather than from free text. `mode` is 1.2.0's one addition to 1.1.0's ten, and the ten are unchanged and in their published order: a class removed would invalidate every pack that pinned it. The file an entry pins must be of the class it declares -- a file of class `mode` validates against `schemas/mode/1.0.0.json` -- which is what stops a pack conferring an artifact of a class it did not name. `profile` is deliberately absent: what it would pin is the whole-house bundle `schemas/profile/1.0.0.json` fixes, and this phase ships the state a behaviour is gated on rather than the bundle that activates it.

trigger.description: A trigger block kind, resolved against the published vocabulary rather than restated here.

condition.description: A condition block kind, resolved against the published vocabulary rather than restated here.

action.description: The action block kind the behaviour ends in. Required, because a behaviour with no action does nothing and the action is the one axis every behaviour the extraction found carries.

priority.description: What arbitration ranks this behaviour by when two behaviours propose for one entity in one tick. A clause of the behaviour rather than of the pack, because one pack's two behaviours may compete at different ranks. Omission takes the default `catalog/pack-policy.yaml` publishes, so a manifest may state what it means and is not required to restate what the default already says.

services.description: The services this behaviour may call, as `domain.service`. The set is the behaviour's declaration of permissions and not a comment on them: the sandbox refuses a call the behaviour's own clause omits, and the pack's effective permission set is computed from these clauses rather than written a second time by hand, so the declaration cannot disagree with the behaviours it describes.

slots.description: The pack-declared slots this behaviour reaches entities through. A clause of the behaviour rather than of the pack, because a pack that declares two slots cannot otherwise say which one a behaviour reads: the sandbox admits a command only through a slot the command's own behaviour names, and a physical button's press is reached the same way rather than through whichever slot the engine happened to visit.

for.description: The name of a `duration` option this behaviour waits out: it proposes only once the reading `match` names has *held* for that long. The run-on period, and the second half of what `match` needs to be useful -- `match: [open]` says the door is open now, and `for: open_minutes` says it has been open for five minutes, which is the difference between an alarm and a nuisance. It names an option rather than carrying a literal duration because *how long* is exactly the sort of number a person wants to change and a manifest author cannot guess: the value resolves under `module.<pack>.<key>` and the panel draws a field for it. A name that is not a declared `duration` option is refused when the manifest is validated -- the clause is meaningless without one, and the check happens where the option list is readable rather than at evaluation, where the reading would silently never hold.

match.description: The readings this behaviour acts on: it proposes only when the entity it acts through currently reads one of these. This is the *value* beside the `condition` kind -- `condition: state` names the kind of test and `match` names what the test is for -- and the pair is what lets a behaviour dispatch rather than fire blind: a vacuum pack starts a clean only when the vacuum reads `docked`, and sends it home only when it reads `cleaning`. A string and not an object, because the comparison is always equality against a literal state name; anything richer would be the expression language `catalog/pack-policy.yaml` forbids. Omitted means 'whatever the slot reads', which is 1.2.0's behaviour and is still a legal pack.

mode.description: The house mode this behaviour enters when it acts, as the frozen mode schema spells a mode name (`schemas/mode/1.0.0.json` lower-cases them). The *value* beside a `service` action for a behaviour whose act is not a device write: the Bedtime button's second clause is the house entering Sleep, and nothing in 1.2.0 could say so -- which is why the pack could not be written. Only the name's *shape* is checked here, and deliberately: a manifest does not know which house it will land in, so the name meets a house for the first time when the behaviour is evaluated. A name the house does not declare is then refused rather than raised -- the request is recorded as a `mode_request` whose `taken` is `false`, the rest of the behaviour still runs, and a tick survives both a pack installed into a house whose modes changed under it and a hand-edited manifest.

scope.description: How often this behaviour is evaluated: once per room it is installed into, or once for the whole house. The corpus records exactly this word per row, and the engine's `BehaviourScope` is that word rather than a translation of it, so the clause is the corpus's own and not a second vocabulary. A behaviour whose acts are about one space -- a room's lights, a room's fan -- is `room`, which is the default and is what 1.2.0 could express. A behaviour about the house as a whole -- the alarm, the doors, the energy meter, the vacuum that cleans everything -- is `house`, and it is evaluated once with the house's own bindings rather than once per room with a room's. `scope` is a clause of the behaviour and not of the pack for the same reason `priority` and `slots` are: one pack may carry both kinds, and a pack-level clause could not say which of its behaviours the word applies to.

suppresses.description: The packs this behaviour holds off while it is on: the module-level override one pack is allowed to place over another, and nothing more. This is the first clause in the manifest that reaches outside the declaring pack -- every other one configures the pack itself -- and what it reaches is the whole of the target's module switch. Deliberately packs and not behaviours, settings or slots: what a suppression does is switch a module off, the one act that changes nothing about the target and is therefore the one act installation can always undo, and a clause that reached further would be a pack editing another pack's configuration -- a state no uninstall can restore and no person can see. Deliberately a declaration and not a log: the manifest says which packs *this* behaviour would hold off, and which of those it is actually holding off right now is derived from which modules are on, which is why suppression is temporary by construction and cannot outlive the switch that caused it. The target need not exist in any particular house -- a manifest does not know which house it will land in -- so a pack may name one it expects beside it, and a house without it simply has nothing held off. A pack naming itself is refused when the manifest is validated: the suppression is derived from what is on, so a pack holding itself off would go off the instant it was on and come back the instant it was off, a module that can never run with no switch anywhere that explains what a person is seeing. Omitted means the behaviour suppresses nothing, which is every 1.3.0 pack and most of 1.4.0.

range.description: The same semver range grammar `engine_api` takes, so a pack author has one range syntax and not two.

default.description: One default string per user-visible name the pack declares: the pack's own name and description, and each declared behaviour's name. The schema requires the block and its non-emptiness; that the keys cover every declared name is checked against the manifest's own `behaviours`, because a static schema cannot name the keys a document will declare.

locales.description: Per-locale overrides, resolved over the default: a locale with no override reads the default, and an override for a string whose default is absent is refused, because an override is a replacement for something and a replacement with nothing behind it is a string that disappears in every other locale.

key.description: The option's name, and the last segment of the setting it resolves under: an option `key: open_minutes` in pack `fridge_guard` is the config key `module.fridge_guard.open_minutes`. The same shape every slot and behaviour name takes, so one name grammar covers the manifest rather than three.

type.description: What kind of value the option takes, which is what decides the control the panel draws: a checkbox for `boolean`, a number field for `integer` and `number`, a select for `enum`, a text field for `string`, and a number field read as a length of time for `duration`. The set is closed rather than the JSON Schema type union, because a control has to be chosen for each and a type outside this list is a control nothing draws. `duration` is `integer` seconds with a unit shown beside it -- a person sets *how long*, and the engine's one use for a duration (`for`) reads it in seconds without parsing a string.

default.description: The value when no layer sets one, and so the bottom of the resolver's stack for this key. Its JSON type is checked against `type` when the manifest is validated rather than here, because a static schema cannot compare one property to another: a `duration`'s default is a whole number of seconds, an `integer`'s a whole number, a `boolean`'s `true` or `false`, an `enum`'s one of its own members.

title.description: The one line a person reads beside the control -- "How long the door may stay open" -- written for somebody who has never opened the manifest. Required, because an option whose only name is its `key` is an option the panel can only label `open_minutes`, which is the defect the whole clause exists to fix.

description.description: The sentence under the title that says what changing it *does*, for when the title is not enough. Optional, because a good title often is enough and a required field would collect filler.

unit.description: The unit shown beside the control for a `number` or `integer` -- `minutes`, `°C`, `%`. Display only, and never parsed: a `duration` is always seconds and says so in its own type rather than through this field, which is what keeps one unit string from meaning a multiplier in one place and a label in another.

minimum.description: The lowest value a `number`, `integer` or `duration` may take, checked when the manifest is validated and applied to the control the panel draws. Absent means unbounded below.

maximum.description: The highest value a `number`, `integer` or `duration` may take, with the same two meanings `minimum` has. Absent means unbounded above.

enum.description: The members a `type: enum` option may take, and required for it -- an enum with no members admits no value at all. Refused on every other type when the manifest is validated, because a member list beside a `boolean` is a clause nobody reads and everybody copies.

name.description: The slot's name. A name the slot vocabulary already carries *reuses* that slot: the pack is asking for the same device every other pack asking for it gets, which is the default. A name the vocabulary does not carry is a slot this pack introduces, and it joins the house's vocabulary when the pack is installed.

accepts_domains.description: Home Assistant domains a binding for this slot may use.

required.description: True when a behaviour of this pack cannot run without it. Ignored for a name the catalog already carries: that slot's own `required` is the catalog's answer and not a pack's.

separate.description: True when this pack wants a device of its own rather than the one every pack naming the slot shares. A separate slot is bound under a pack-qualified key, so two packs may each hold their own motion sensor while a third shares the room's.
